nodes.label: SEC
beginner: The main watchdog for the stock market and public companies.
Forces honest financial disclosure and punishes fraud and insider trading.
expert: Regulates securities markets, exchanges, brokers, and investment advisers under the 1933 and 1934 Acts.
Requires public-company filings (10-K, 10-Q, 8-K) that anchor equity and credit valuation.
Oversees mutual funds and, jointly with the CFTC, parts of the derivatives market.
Source: SEC.

nodes.label: CFTC
beginner: The watchdog for futures, options, and derivatives markets.
Makes sure commodity and derivatives trading is fair and transparent.
expert: Regulates US derivatives, including a swaps market of roughly $600T+ notional (BIS).
Oversees futures exchanges (CME) and mandated central clearing after the 2008 crisis.
Splits oversight of some hybrid products with the SEC.
Source: CFTC, BIS.

nodes.label: FDIC
beginner: Insures your bank deposits so you do not lose savings if a bank fails.
Steps in to close and sell failed banks.
expert: Insures deposits up to $250,000 per depositor, per bank, per ownership category.
Backs over $10T of insured deposits through the Deposit Insurance Fund.
Resolved Silicon Valley Bank and Signature Bank in March 2023, backstopping uninsured depositors.
Source: FDIC.

nodes.label: US Treasury
beginner: The US government borrows money by selling bonds.
The interest rate on those bonds ripples through every other rate in finance.
expert: Issues T-Bills (1yr or less), Notes (2 to 10yr), and Bonds (20 to 30yr).
US debt outstanding is roughly $35T as of 2024.
Auctions weekly, with primary dealers required to bid.
Source: US Treasury, TreasuryDirect.

nodes.label: Federal Reserve
beginner: The central bank that controls interest rates and money supply.
It keeps prices stable, supports jobs, and lends as a last resort in crises.
expert: Sets policy via the Fed Funds target, balance-sheet policy (QE/QT), and forward guidance.
Balance sheet peaked near $8.9T in 2022 (FRED: WALCL).
Backstops the system through the discount window and emergency facilities.
Source: Federal Reserve, FRED.

nodes.label: FOMC
beginner: The committee that votes on interest-rate changes.
Meets and votes eight times a year.
expert: Federal Open Market Committee: 12 voting members set the Fed Funds target range.
CME FedWatch tracks hike/hold/cut odds across 25bps buckets.
Source: Federal Reserve, CME.

nodes.label: Fed Funds Rate
beginner: The main interest rate the Fed controls.
Almost every other rate in finance takes its cue from this number.
expert: Overnight interbank lending rate, targeted as a range by the FOMC.
Transmits to the economy through the yield curve, credit spreads, and mortgage rates.
Source: FRED (FEDFUNDS, EFFR).

nodes.label: Commercial Banks
beginner: Where households and businesses deposit money and take out loans.
They turn deposits into loans, which creates most money, but that makes them vulnerable to runs.
expert: Roughly 4,000 FDIC-insured banks; the top four hold about 40% of deposits.
Create money via fractional-reserve lending and transmit Fed policy to the real economy.
Silicon Valley Bank failed in March 2023 after a $42B one-day deposit run.
Regulated jointly by the Fed, OCC, and FDIC. Source: FDIC, Federal Reserve.

nodes.label: Primary Dealers
beginner: A small group of large banks required to buy government bonds at auction.
They are the pipes that move new government debt into the market, so if they pull back, yields spike.
expert: 25 primary dealers as of 2024 (NY Fed), including Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan, and Citigroup.
Obligated to bid at every Treasury auction and make markets in Treasuries.
Serve as the Fed counterparties that execute QE and QT.
Post-2008 leverage rules (SLR) can cap how many bonds they absorb. Source: NY Fed, BIS.

nodes.label: Repo Market
beginner: The overnight market where banks and funds borrow cash using bonds as collateral.
It is the plumbing of short-term funding, and the Fed steps in when it seizes.
expert: Roughly $4T+ in daily US repo transactions, the core of short-term funding.
The Sept 2019 repo spike (rates near 10%) forced emergency Fed intervention.
The Fed reverse-repo (RRP) facility peaked above $2.5T in late 2022 (FRED: RRPONTSYD).
SOFR, the LIBOR successor, is derived from overnight repo rates. Source: NY Fed, FRED.

nodes.label: Money Market Funds
beginner: Funds that hold very safe short-term assets and act like cash for big investors.
They are major lenders into the repo market and can spread stress if investors pull out fast.
expert: Roughly $6.5T in US money-market fund assets as of 2024 (ICI).
The Reserve Primary Fund broke the buck in 2008, freezing short-term funding.
Large supplier of cash to the Fed RRP facility and the repo market.
Yields track the Fed Funds Rate closely. Source: ICI, OFR.

nodes.label: Hedge Funds / Leverage
beginner: Lightly regulated funds that use borrowed money to amplify their bets.
They add liquidity in calm times but can worsen crashes when forced to sell.
expert: Roughly $4T+ in global hedge-fund assets, heavy users of repo leverage.
The Treasury basis trade (leveraged long cash, short futures) is a flagged systemic risk.
Forced deleveraging amplified the March 2020 Treasury-market dislocation.
Source: Fed Financial Stability Report, BIS.

nodes.label: Fannie Mae & Freddie Mac
beginner: Government-sponsored companies that buy mortgages from banks and package them into bonds.
They stand behind about half of all US home loans and have been government-controlled since 2008.
expert: Guarantee and issue roughly $7T of agency mortgage-backed securities.
Put into FHFA conservatorship in Sept 2008 and still government-controlled.
Their MBS form the second-largest US bond market after Treasuries.
Source: FHFA, SIFMA.

nodes.label: Yield Curve
beginner: A chart of government borrowing rates across different time lengths.
When short-term rates exceed long-term (inverted), recession risk rises.
expert: Plots Treasury yields against maturity.
The 2Y/10Y inversion has preceded all eight recessions since 1955 (FRED: T10Y2Y).
Tracked here via US2Y vs US10Y. Source: FRED.

nodes.label: Credit Markets
beginner: The market where companies borrow money.
When borrowing gets more expensive, businesses invest and hire less.
expert: Investment-grade plus high-yield corporate bonds, over $10T outstanding.
The option-adjusted spread (OAS) over Treasuries widens during stress.
Source: FRED (ICE BofA OAS indices).

nodes.label: Equity Markets
beginner: The stock market.
Higher interest rates make stocks less valuable by discounting future profits more heavily.
expert: S&P 500 and Nasdaq, roughly $45T total US market cap.
Equity risk premium equals earnings yield minus the risk-free rate.
Rising rates compress multiples through the DCF denominator. Source: FactSet, FRED.

nodes.label: Mortgage / MBS Market
beginner: The market for bonds backed by bundles of home loans.
It sets the mortgage rate households actually pay and closely follows Fed policy and long-term yields.
expert: Roughly $12T of agency MBS outstanding (SIFMA), pricing 30-year mortgage rates.
The Fed held about $2.6T of MBS at its 2022 peak via QE (FRED: WSHOMCB).
Mortgage rates roughly track the 10Y Treasury plus a spread. Source: SIFMA, FRED.

nodes.label: Tech Equities
beginner: Tech stocks are hit hardest by rising rates.
Their profits sit far in the future, so a higher discount rate cuts their value most.
expert: Long-duration assets, the most sensitive to discount-rate moves.
The megacap tech complex carries roughly 28% weight in the S&P 500 (2024).
Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices.

nodes.label: Financials
beginner: Banks and financial firms.
They benefit from higher rates if lending rates rise faster than deposit costs.
expert: Net interest margin expands when the yield curve steepens.
A rising 2Y squeezes short-term funding costs.
KBW Bank Index ($BKX) is the sector benchmark. Source: FRED, S&P.

nodes.label: Defensive Equities
beginner: Stable companies like utilities, groceries, and healthcare.
Investors flock to them when markets turn scary.
expert: Utilities, staples, and healthcare, low beta near 0.4 to 0.6 vs the S&P 500.
Stable dividends get bid up in risk-off rotations.
Typically outperform late in the cycle. Source: sector rotation research.

nodes.label: Core CPI
beginner: The inflation rate, excluding volatile food and energy.
When prices rise too fast, the Fed raises rates to cool the economy.
expert: CPI ex-food and energy. The Fed targets 2% PCE, which CPI tracks closely.
A persistent overshoot drives a tightening cycle and higher real rates.
Source: BLS monthly release.

nodes.label: Non-Farm Payrolls
beginner: The monthly US jobs report.
Too many jobs signals inflation risk, too few signals recession risk.
expert: BLS first-Friday release, central to the Fed dual mandate.
Strong payrolls plus high CPI push the FOMC hawkish.
Roughly 158M employed as of mid-2024 — a level figure typed in by hand, not refreshed daily.
Source: BLS Current Employment Statistics (series CES0000000001).

nodes.label: VIX
beginner: The 'fear index', measuring how nervous options traders are.
Above 30 signals panic and a rush out of stocks.
expert: Cboe Volatility Index, the implied 30-day volatility of the S&P 500.
Above 20 is elevated anxiety, above 30 marks a crisis or risk-off regime.

Inverse correlation to the S&P near -0.74 in long samples. The -0.74 is a long-run figure with no window stated here; the daily-change relationship on this map is fitted separately and shown on the vix-to-equities link.
Source: Cboe (index methodology and historical series).

nodes.label: US Dollar (DXY)
beginner: The dollar measured against a basket of major foreign currencies.
A stronger dollar makes US exports pricier and imports cheaper.
expert: DXY is trade-weighted against six currencies (EUR 57.6%, JPY 13.6%, GBP 11.9%, CAD, SEK, CHF). The weights are fixed by the index rules, not re-estimated.
A strong dollar tightens global financial conditions.
The dollar remains the dominant reserve currency, though its share of allocated global FX reserves has been on a slow structural decline for over two decades — tracked live here.
Source: ICE (DXY index weights); IMF COFER (allocated reserve currency shares).
Roughly 40 to 50% of trade invoices were in USD as of 2022 (no live source for this figure).
Source: BIS (trade invoicing currency shares, 2022).

nodes.label: EM FX / Global FX
beginner: Exchange rates between the dollar and developing-country currencies.
A rising dollar stresses countries with dollar-denominated debt.
expert: EM nations owed roughly $5.5T in USD external debt as of 2023.
A 10% USD appreciation historically cuts EM GDP about 1.5%.
Dollar strength drives capital flight, EM rate hikes, and contagion risk.
Source: IIF Global Debt Monitor (2023); IMF WP/19/25 (the 1.5% elasticity).

nodes.label: Gold
beginner: A 'safe haven' asset bought when people fear inflation or crashes.
Its price often moves opposite to the dollar.
expert: Near-zero long-run correlation to equities, which is the basis of the diversification case.
Key drivers: real rates (inverse), USD (inverse), inflation expectations, geopolitics.

Central banks have been structural net buyers of gold in most years for over a decade, a shift in reserve composition tracked live here across the largest public holders. Real rates (TIPS) still dominate day-to-day price moves.
Source: IMF International Reserves and Foreign Currency Liquidity (IRFCL); the dollar link on this map is fitted separately.

nodes.label: Oil Price (WTI)
beginner: Energy is an input cost for nearly everything.
Rising oil directly feeds higher inflation.
expert: WTI is the US benchmark, Brent the global one. Oil is roughly 3.5% of US CPI.
OPEC+ controls about 40% of global production.
A $10/bbl rise adds roughly 0.3 to 0.4% to headline CPI (IMF). Source: EIA, IMF.

nodes.label: China Economy
beginner: The world's second-largest economy and a top US trading partner.
When China slows, US exports fall and commodity prices drop.
expert: Held roughly $780B of US Treasuries as of 2024, down from a $1.3T peak.
GDP near $18T as of 2023, bilateral US trade near $575B/year.
Taiwan Strait risk threatens semiconductors: Taiwan makes the large majority of leading-edge (sub-7nm) chips. The often-quoted ~92% share is an industry estimate, not an official statistic.
Source: US Treasury TIC (holdings, monthly); IMF WEO (GDP, 2023); the chip-share figure has no single official dataset.

nodes.label: Russia / Sanctions
beginner: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine triggered massive sanctions.
That cut energy supplies to Europe and spiked oil and gas prices globally.
expert: Controlled roughly 12% of global oil and 17% of natural gas supply as of 2022.
Post-2022 sanctions immobilised about $300B of Russian central-bank reserves, per the statements of the freezing governments.
Redirected energy to China and India via a shadow tanker fleet, rewiring trade flows.
Source: IEA (supply shares, 2022); EU and G7 official statements (the reserve figure); IEA oil market reports (redirected flows).

nodes.label: Global Trade / WTO
beginner: The rules that govern how countries trade with each other.
When trade breaks down through tariffs or wars, prices rise everywhere.
expert: Global goods trade was roughly $25T/year as of 2023.
US tariffs on Chinese goods rose from about 3% to 19% between 2018 and 2024.
Post-COVID supply-chain breaks are estimated to have added 1.5 to 2% to global CPI in 2021 to 2022 — a modelled range from central-bank research, not a measured series.
Source: WTO (trade volume, 2023); PIIE tariff tracker (tariff rates); IMF and ECB research (the CPI contribution estimate).

nodes.label: Bank Deposits
beginner: The money in your checking and savings accounts.
To a bank it is a debt it owes you; for the economy it is most of the money that exists, created when banks make loans.
expert: Commercial-bank deposits (~$17-18T) are the largest component of the money supply and are created endogenously: a new loan credits a matching deposit.
They are bank liabilities, insured by the FDIC to $250k, and their flows drive bank funding costs and the reserves/RRP split.
Deposit flight forced the March 2023 SVB and Signature failures.
Source: FRED DPSACBW027SBOG, FDIC.

nodes.label: Money Supply (M2)
beginner: The total pool of spendable money in the economy: cash plus checking, savings and money-market balances.
When it grows far faster than the economy, inflation usually follows.
expert: M2 (~$21T) = currency + checkable and savings deposits + small time deposits + retail money-fund shares.
It grew about 40% in 2020-22, then posted its first year-on-year contraction since 1948 in 2023.
The quantity-theory link to prices is loose but nonzero; a watched, lagging inflation input.
Source: FRED M2SL.

nodes.label: Mortgage Rates (30Y)
beginner: The interest rate on a typical 30-year home loan, the single most important number for US housing.
It tracks the 10-year Treasury yield plus a spread, not the Fed policy rate directly.
expert: The 30-year fixed rate is roughly the 10-year Treasury yield plus a 1.5-3% primary-secondary spread, priced off current-coupon MBS rather than the fed funds rate.
It peaked near 7.8% in October 2023 and is the dominant channel from rates to household balance sheets.
High rates create a lock-in effect that freezes existing owners in place.
Source: FRED MORTGAGE30US, Freddie Mac PMMS.

nodes.label: Private Credit
beginner: Loans made directly by investment funds instead of banks, usually to mid-sized companies.
It has grown into a multi-trillion-dollar shadow lending industry.
expert: Direct-lending and private-credit funds (~$1.6-1.7T AUM) lend to middle-market and PE-owned firms at floating rates.
Largely unregulated, illiquid and marked to model, the sector filled space left by post-crisis bank retrenchment.
Its main backers are insurers and pensions, and it is untested through a full default cycle.
Source: IMF GFSR, industry estimates.

nodes.label: T-Bills
beginner: Short-term US government IOUs that mature in a year or less.
The safest, most liquid dollar asset — the base of the money market.
expert: Treasury bills (<=1yr) are the collateral and cash-management backbone of money markets; ~$6T outstanding.
Bill supply swings with the deficit and the debt ceiling and drives money-fund allocation between bills and the Fed.
Source: US Treasury, SIFMA.

nodes.label: Listed Options
beginner: Exchange-traded contracts to buy or sell stocks at a set price.
Used to hedge or speculate; their pricing is where the VIX comes from.
expert: Listed equity/index options clear through the OCC; dealer hedging (gamma) can amplify or dampen index moves.
The VIX is computed from S&P 500 option prices, so options ARE the volatility signal.
Source: OCC, Cboe.

nodes.label: ETFs / Index Funds
beginner: Baskets of stocks or bonds you can trade like a single share.
Most new investing money flows through them, shaping which assets rise.
expert: Index funds/ETFs held 57% of combined equity fund assets as of Sept 2024; creation/redemption ties ETF prices to the underlying.
Concentrated flows move whole indices and can propagate stress in illiquid underlyings (e.g. HY bond ETFs).
Source: ICI Release: Active and Index Investing, Sept 2024; Fed staff research, FEDS 2018-060 (index-inclusion effects, Section 2.4).

nodes.label: Energy Sector
beginner: Oil and gas company stocks.
They rise and fall mostly with the price of oil.
expert: Energy equities are the primary equity-market conduit for oil-price moves and a partial inflation hedge.
Roughly 4% of the S&P 500 by weight but a major swing factor in earnings during oil shocks.
Source: S&P Dow Jones Indices, EIA.

nodes.label: Households
beginner: You and every other consumer.
Household spending is about two-thirds of the whole economy.
expert: Household balance sheets link mortgage rates, credit and equity/house wealth to consumption (~68% of GDP).
Debt-service ratios and confidence transmit financial conditions into real demand.
Source: BEA, Fed Z.1, NY Fed Household Debt report.

links.why: The Fed Board chairs and dominates the FOMC, setting the agenda for the committee votes.
links.stat: Structural control link, not a measured correlation. Source: Federal Reserve Act. Tested over 40 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=0.0 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: The FOMC directly votes the Fed Funds target range up or down eight times a year.
links.stat: Definitional link. The FOMC vote IS the rate. Definitional, not measured: the FOMC vote sets the target rate.

links.why: A higher policy rate lifts the whole curve, especially the short end, since all borrowing is priced off the risk-free rate.
links.stat: The 2Y tracks the expected policy path, correlation above 0.9 (FRED: FEDFUNDS vs DGS2). Tested over 198 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=1.3 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: Higher base rates raise corporate borrowing costs and widen spreads as default risk rises.
links.stat: HY spreads widen with hikes, correlation strengthens in tightening cycles (FRED: BAMLH0A0HYM2). Tested over 208 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=0.2 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: The Fed exists to cool inflation. Tighter policy reduces CPI over time.
links.stat: Effect runs on a 12 to 18 month lag, so it is not a same-period correlation. This is a standard, widely accepted monetary-policy stylized fact (the "long and variable lags" of transmission) rather than a single citable study.

links.why: Treasury sets bond supply. Heavier issuance pushes yields up as buyers demand more to absorb it.
links.stat: Supply matters at the margin via the term premium. The NY Fed ACM (Adrian-Crump-Moench) model is the standard tool for measuring term premium, though it measures the premium itself rather than directly demonstrating that issuance drives it; the causal step is standard fixed-income economics.

links.why: Every new bond flows through the primary dealers who are required to bid.
links.stat: Structural link. 26 dealers are mandated auction bidders as of Jan 2026, up from 25 (NY Fed).

links.why: The Fed executes QE and QT by buying and selling with the primary dealers.
links.stat: Structural link. Dealers are the Fed open-market counterparties (NY Fed).

links.why: The Fed is lender of last resort through the discount window and emergency facilities.
links.stat: Structural backstop. The 2023 BTFP facility helped stem the regional-bank run (Federal Reserve); First Republic still failed in a continued run about two months after BTFP launched, so it contained rather than fully stopped the contagion.

links.why: Higher rates mark down the long bonds banks bought when rates were near zero. The loss is invisible while the bonds are held to maturity, and instantly real the moment a deposit run forces a sale.
links.stat: US banks carried roughly $620.4B of UNREALISED losses on securities in Q4 2022; $515B, a commonly cited figure, is actually the Q1 2023 total, a different quarter. Source: FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile. This is the mechanism, not a correlation.

links.why: Dealers absorb Treasury supply. When their balance sheets are constrained, they demand a bigger concession to take bonds, so yields rise and liquidity thins.
links.stat: Dealer balance-sheet capacity is a recognised driver of Treasury market liquidity. Source: NY Fed, OFR. Magnitude unquantified.

links.why: Bank lending standards decide how much credit reaches the economy.
links.stat: Tightening loan standards precede credit contraction (Fed Senior Loan Officer Survey).

links.why: Banks are the core of the financials sector, so bank health drives the sector.
links.stat: The KBW Bank Index is bank-dominated. Near 1-for-1 co-movement. True by index construction, not a measured correlation: the KBW Bank Index is bank-dominated.

links.why: The Fed sets a floor under repo through its standing facilities, lending against collateral when private cash will not.
links.stat: The Standing Repo Facility and reverse repo facility bracket the effective rate. Source: NY Fed. Fitted over 40 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=+2.23e-06, |t|=2.6.

links.why: Repo is a core source of short-term funding for banks and dealers.
links.stat: A 2019 repo seizure forced Fed intervention to keep banks funded (NY Fed).

links.why: Hedge funds run leveraged basis trades financed in repo. A rise in haircuts forces deleveraging, which was a key contributor to what broke the Treasury market in March 2020, alongside a broader dash-for-cash and dealer balance-sheet constraints.
links.stat: The cash-futures basis trade is repo-financed and has been flagged as a systemic vulnerability. Source: BIS, OFR, Fed FSR.

links.why: Money market funds are the largest cash lenders in repo. When they swell, they park the cash in repo and at the Fed rather than lending it to banks.
links.stat: MMFs were the dominant counterparty in the Fed’s reverse repo facility, which peaked above $2.5T in 2022–23. Source: NY Fed.

links.why: Money funds are major buyers of short-term Treasury bills.
links.stat: MMFs hold a large share of the T-bill market (ICI, Treasury).

links.why: When the policy rate rises, money market funds pass it straight through to savers while bank deposits lag badly. Cash walks out of banks and into MMFs.
links.stat: MMF assets grew past $6T during the 2022–23 hiking cycle while bank deposits fell. Source: OFR money market fund monitor, ICI.

links.why: Leveraged basis trades amplify Treasury moves in whichever direction they unwind.
links.stat: Sign is regime-dependent. Deleveraging worsened the March 2020 dislocation (Fed, BIS).

links.why: Fannie and Freddie guarantee and securitise the mortgages that become agency MBS. Without the guarantee the market would not exist at its current size.
links.stat: GSEs backstop the bulk of the US mortgage market, cited at roughly $12T in FHFA testimony; total 1-4 family mortgage debt outstanding has since grown to about $14.6T (2025, Fed/Statista). Source: FHFA, SIFMA.

links.why: Deposit insurance is what stops a run. It only works up to the limit, which is why UNINSURED deposits are the ones that flee.
links.stat: FDIC insures $250k per depositor per bank. SVB was roughly 94% uninsured, which is why its run was so fast. Source: FDIC.

links.why: Mandatory disclosure and anti-fraud enforcement underpin trust in the stock market.
links.stat: Structural link. Disclosure supports equity-market integrity (SEC).

links.why: The same disclosure rules make the corporate-bond market transparent.
links.stat: Structural link (SEC).

links.why: The CFTC oversees the futures exchanges where oil prices are actually set.
links.stat: Structural link. Oil is discovered in CFTC-regulated futures (CME).

links.why: Rising Treasury yields raise the baseline that corporate bonds are priced against.
links.stat: Corporate yields = Treasury yield + spread. Structural pricing baseline. Fitted over 198 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=-0.3013, |t|=2.8.

links.why: Higher yields raise the discount rate in stock valuations, compressing multiples.
links.stat: Regime-dependent. Strongly negative in the 2022 rate shock, often positive in growth booms. No stable coefficient. Fitted over 197 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=-0.02869, |t|=2.0.

links.why: A steeper curve widens bank net interest margins (borrow short, lend long).
links.stat: Bank stocks track curve steepness loosely (FRED: T10Y2Y vs $BKX). Tested over 197 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=0.4 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: MBS prices fall as yields rise, and they fall FASTER than plain bonds because rising rates also stop prepayment, stretching the bond’s duration exactly when you least want it.
links.stat: This is negative convexity, and it is the reason bank MBS books were hit harder than their Treasury books in 2022. Source: SIFMA, Fed FSR.

links.why: Tight credit spreads signal confidence and easy corporate funding, which supports stocks.
links.stat: HY spreads and the S&P move inversely, roughly -0.5 to -0.7 depending on the period (wider in stress episodes, tighter in calm markets). Tighter spreads lift equities (FRED). Fitted over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=-0.08569, |t|=12.5. The sign shown is the fitted one; the earlier hand sign was +1.
links.fieldNote: I originally had wider credit spreads lifting stocks — which, looking back, never made sense. Once I actually measured it, spreads widening tracks equities falling, the way you’d expect.

links.why: Tech is a high-beta slice of the broad market and amplifies its direction.
links.stat: Nasdaq-100 beta to the S&P is roughly 1.2 to 1.3. Fitted over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=+0.000231, |t|=28.3.

links.why: Financials move with the broad market plus their own rate sensitivity.
links.stat: Financials beta to the S&P is roughly 1.1. Fitted over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=+0.0001131, |t|=11.9.

links.why: Defensives rise in rallies but with lower beta, lagging up and cushioning down.
links.stat: Defensive beta is roughly 0.4 to 0.6 vs the S&P. Tested over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: no significant daily-frequency relationship (|t|=0.8). The mechanism is sourced; the magnitude is not measured here.

links.why: Tech earnings sit far in the future, so a higher discount rate hits them hardest.
links.stat: 2022: the Nasdaq fell about 33% (confirmed across market recaps) as the 2Y (FRED DGS2) rose roughly 320 to 370bps depending on the reference window — from the yield trough to year-end, versus calendar year-open to year-end. Tested over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=0.3 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: The fear gauge rising means investors are selling stocks.
links.stat: VIX and S&P daily returns correlate roughly -0.74 (CBOE). Fitted over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=-0.004172, |t|=22.2.

links.why: When fear rises, money rotates toward defensive sectors like utilities and staples - so they fall LESS than the market, but in absolute terms they still fall.
links.stat: Relative defensive outperformance in risk-off episodes, not absolute gains (sector rotation research). Fitted over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=-0.0007325, |t|=2.0. The sign shown is the fitted one; the earlier hand sign was +1.

links.why: High inflation pushes the FOMC toward a hawkish, rate-hiking stance.
links.stat: The 2021 to 2023 CPI overshoot drove 525bps of hikes (Federal Reserve). Tested over 57 month-over-month changes in a 6-year offline calibration window (calibration_report_multiyear.txt): the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=1.1 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: A hot jobs report signals an overheating economy and pushes the FOMC to tighten.
links.stat: Payroll surprises move hike odds via the dual mandate (BLS, CME FedWatch). Tested over 57 month-over-month changes in a 6-year offline calibration window (calibration_report_multiyear.txt): no significant relationship (|t|=0.5).

links.why: Higher US rates attract global capital seeking yield, raising demand for dollars.
links.stat: DXY rose about 19% from its 2022 trough to its intra-year peak alongside the hiking cycle (ICE), but gave back nearly 10% in Q4; the full calendar-year close-to-close change was a more modest ~9.4% (94.63 to 103.52). Tested over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=0.6 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: A strong dollar weakens EM currencies and makes their dollar debt costlier.
links.stat: A 10% USD rise historically cuts EM GDP about 1.9% (IMF WP/15/179, "Collateral Damage: Dollar Strength and Emerging Markets’ Growth"). Note: WP/19/25 is sometimes miscited here — that paper is actually about fuel-price competitiveness, unrelated to this claim.

links.why: Gold is priced in dollars and pays no yield, so a stronger dollar makes it less attractive.
links.stat: Long-run USD/gold correlation is roughly -0.4 to -0.6 (WGC). Fitted over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=-0.01465, |t|=4.4.

links.why: Crude is priced in dollars, so a stronger dollar makes it pricier for foreign buyers - which argues for an inverse link.
links.stat: Long-run studies find a weak inverse link, roughly -0.3 (EIA). Fitted over 198 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=+0.02732, |t|=4.7. The sign shown is the fitted one; the earlier hand sign was -1. The textbook dollar-pricing channel is negative, so this window reads as a demand-led regime rather than a refutation.
links.fieldNote: I had this coded as dollar up → oil down — the textbook FX-pricing story everyone learns. The data disagreed. Over this window it’s actually positive. I’m leaving that in and telling you it’s weird rather than hiding it.

links.why: Roughly 40% of S&P revenue is foreign, so a strong dollar shrinks it once converted back.
links.stat: A recurring EPS headwind in earnings seasons (FactSet). Fitted over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=-0.004636, |t|=3.2.

links.why: Stronger EM currencies ease dollar-debt burdens and global risk appetite, which supports credit conditions.
links.stat: Spillover concentrated in risk-off episodes. Tested over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: no significant daily-frequency relationship (|t|=0.4). The mechanism is sourced; the magnitude is not measured here.

links.why: Oil is the single largest non-housing input into inflation.
links.stat: The underlying rule of thumb is percentage-based: roughly a 10% oil-price rise adds 0.3 to 0.4% to headline CPI (IMF and corroborating Fed research). A $10/bbl move only equals about 10% when oil is near $100/bbl; at today’s roughly $65 to $90/bbl range, $10 is closer to an 11 to 15% move. Tested over 38 month-over-month changes in a 6-year offline calibration window (calibration_report_multiyear.txt): no significant relationship (|t|=0.6).

links.why: Spiking fear drives safe-haven demand into gold.
links.stat: Regime-dependent co-movement, strongest in risk-off episodes (WGC). Tested over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=1.2 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: High oil is a tax on consumers and raises input costs, squeezing margins.
links.stat: Effect concentrated at high price levels. Sign is regime-dependent (energy shock research), but the inverse sign shown here held over the fitted window. Fitted over 198 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=-0.0009408, |t|=5.1.
links.fieldNote: This inverse sign looks tidy, but I don’t fully trust it — oil and equities flip correlation depending on whether a rally is demand-led or supply-led, and this fitted window just happened to land on the textbook side.

links.why: Gold and Treasuries are both flight-to-safety assets bid together in stress.
links.stat: Weak co-movement overall, stronger in risk-off. Unverified causal direction. Tested over 197 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=1.7 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: Russia supplies about 12% of global oil, so sanctions or cuts remove barrels and spike prices.
links.stat: The 2022 invasion pushed Brent above $120/bbl (IEA, EIA).

links.why: Conflict drives safe-haven demand for gold.
links.stat: Geopolitical premium in gold during 2022 (WGC).

links.why: China strength cuts both ways. Growth lifts multinational revenue, while tension and tariffs squeeze margins.
links.stat: No stable sign. Tariff escalation pressured S&P multinationals in 2018 to 2019, while China demand supported earnings in expansions (PIIE, FactSet).

links.why: China holds about $659B of Treasuries, down from roughly $780B a couple of years ago. If it sells, Treasury prices fall and yields rise.
links.stat: China holdings fell from a $1.3T peak (Nov 2013) to ~$659B (US Treasury TIC data, May 2026, the most recent available). Price impact unverified. No free daily series for the price impact: TIC holdings are monthly.

links.why: China is the largest crude importer, so stronger growth lifts global oil demand.
links.stat: China drove over 60% of global oil-demand growth from 2013 to 2023, but IEA reporting now shows that share fell below 20% of 2024’s rise, with India projected to lead demand growth through the decade instead (EIA, IEA).

links.why: Trade and shipping-route disruptions constrain oil supply and lift prices.
links.stat: Route disruptions add a risk premium to crude (IEA).

links.why: Tariffs and supply-chain breaks raise import costs, feeding directly into inflation.
links.stat: IMF research (WP 22/031) finds supply-chain disruptions added about 1% to global core inflation specifically in 2021; other estimates for the broader 2021 to 2022 window and different inflation measures range higher (IMF, PIIE).

links.why: Trade-policy uncertainty makes lenders cautious and widens spreads.
links.stat: Uncertainty premium in spreads during trade escalations is the standard view (IMF GFSR, central-bank commentary). The Caldara & Iacoviello Geopolitical Risk (GPR) Index (policyuncertainty.com/gpr.html) is a free, regularly updated dataset now available to test this; a 2025 study regressing GPR against credit-spread panels found a small average spread DECREASE associated with a 1-SD GPR rise, complicating the simple "uncertainty widens spreads" reading even though it remains the mainstream mechanism.

links.why: Russia sanctions rewired trade rules and energy flows, intensifying overall disruption.
links.stat: Structural regime shift in global trade (WTO, IEA).

links.why: US-China policy effectively sets the global trade regime, so escalation raises systemic tension.
links.stat: Structural driver of the trade regime (WTO, PIIE).

links.why: Bank lending creates deposits: a new loan credits the borrower's account, so credit expansion is literally money creation.
links.stat: Endogenous money view. Source: Bank of England, Money creation in the modern economy (2014).

links.why: Deposits are banks' cheapest and largest funding source; a stable deposit base is what lets banks lend and hold assets.
links.stat: Deposits fund the bulk of US bank balance sheets. Source: FDIC.

links.why: Checkable and savings deposits are the largest component of M2, so deposit growth mechanically expands the money supply.
links.stat: Deposits are the dominant M2 component. Source: FRED M2SL.

links.why: FDIC insurance to $250k makes deposits money-good, preventing runs and keeping the deposit base stable.
links.stat: Insures roughly $10T of deposits via the DIF. Source: FDIC.

links.why: When policy rates rise above sticky deposit rates, cash flows out of deposits into higher-yielding money funds and T-bills (deposit disintermediation).
links.stat: The 2022-23 cycle drove record flows from deposits to money funds. Source: Fed H.8, ICI.

links.why: Tighter policy slows credit and drains liquidity, so faster rate hikes coincide with slower or negative broad-money growth.
links.stat: M2 contracted year-on-year in 2023 during the hiking cycle. Source: FRED M2SL. Fitted over 57 month-over-month changes in a 6-year offline calibration window (calibration_history.json, not data.json — see calibration_report_multiyear.txt): slope=-0.0098219, |t|=3.3.

links.why: Broad-money growth well above output tends to feed inflation with a long, variable lag (loose quantity-theory channel).
links.stat: The 2020-22 M2 surge preceded the inflation spike; the link is loose. Source: FRED M2SL, CPIAUCSL. Fitted over 58 month-over-month changes in a 6-year offline calibration window (calibration_history.json, not data.json — see calibration_report_multiyear.txt): slope=+0.0011811, |t|=3.5.

links.why: Rapid money-supply growth stokes debasement and inflation fears, a core part of the bull case for gold as a monetary hedge.
links.stat: Directional; magnitude unquantified. Source: WGC. Tested over 38 month-over-month changes in a 6-year offline calibration window (calibration_report_multiyear.txt): no significant relationship (|t|=0.7).

links.why: The 30-year mortgage is priced off the 10-year Treasury plus a spread, so long-end yields, not the fed funds rate, set mortgage costs.
links.stat: Mortgage rate tracks the 10Y with a 1.5 to 3% spread. Source: FRED MORTGAGE30US vs DGS10. Fitted over 40 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=+0.2892, |t|=2.4.

links.why: Lenders price loans off where they can sell the resulting MBS, so wider MBS spreads push mortgage rates above Treasuries.
links.stat: The primary-secondary spread widens with MBS stress. Source: Freddie Mac PMMS.

links.why: Policy rates reach mortgages only indirectly, via the long end and MBS spreads: a weak, lagged link, not a direct peg.
links.stat: Mortgage rates can move opposite the fed funds rate. Source: FRED. Tested over 40 usable daily changes in the train split: no significant daily-frequency relationship (|t|=0.5). The mechanism is sourced; the magnitude is not measured here.

links.why: Housing is the largest household credit market, so higher mortgage rates freeze sales and refinancing and tighten overall credit conditions.
links.stat: Mortgage debt is the biggest US household liability. Source: NY Fed Household Debt report. Fitted over 40 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=+0.5232, |t|=2.0. The sign shown is the fitted one; the earlier hand sign was -1.

links.why: Private credit now rivals bank and bond lending as a source of corporate credit, so its expansion loosens overall financial conditions.
links.stat: Roughly $1.6 to 1.7T AUM as of mid-2023 (IMF GFSR, April 2024 Chapter 2). Current 2026 industry estimates put private-credit AUM well above $2T, heading toward roughly $4T by 2030 (Moody’s, Morgan Stanley), reflecting continued ~20%/year growth off that base rather than a static figure.

links.why: Floating-rate loans mean higher policy rates lift fund yields but also raise borrower default risk: a two-sided effect.
links.stat: Conditional sign. Source: IMF GFSR 2024.

links.why: As banks retrench from middle-market lending after Dodd-Frank, private credit expands to fill the gap, so bank pullback grows the sector.
links.stat: The sector grew as banks' leveraged-lending share fell. Source: IMF GFSR.

links.why: Private credit sits inside the same asset-management complex; funds and their investors channel capital into direct lending in search of yield.
links.stat: Directional; magnitude unquantified. Source: industry estimates. "Industry estimates" names no dataset, so the magnitude is unsourced.

links.why: The Treasury issues bills to fund the deficit and manage cash; issuance sets bill supply.
links.stat: ~$6T bills outstanding. Source: US Treasury, SIFMA. Fitted over 198 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=+0.1431, |t|=4.6.

links.why: Money-market funds hold bills as their core asset, so bill supply drives fund allocation and yields.
links.stat: Bills are the largest MMF holding. Source: ICI, OFR.

links.why: Bill yields track the Fed funds rate almost one-for-one at the front end.
links.stat: T-bill yields ~= policy rate. Source: FRED DTB3 vs FEDFUNDS. Tested over 198 usable daily changes in the train split: no significant daily-frequency relationship (|t|=0.4). The mechanism is sourced; the magnitude is not measured here.

links.why: The VIX is derived from S&P 500 option prices, so option-implied vol IS the fear gauge.
links.stat: VIX = 30-day implied vol from SPX options. Source: Cboe.

links.why: Dealer option hedging (gamma) can amplify or dampen index moves depending on positioning.
links.stat: Conditional sign. Source: OCC, dealer-gamma research.

links.why: ETFs hold the equity market; index levels drive ETF NAVs via creation/redemption.
links.stat: Index funds/ETFs held 57% of combined domestic+world equity fund assets as of Sept 2024 (computed from ICI’s own active/index totals). Passive share of all long-term fund assets: 19% in 2010 → 52% in 2025. Source: ICI Release: Active and Index Investing, Sept 2024; ICI 2026 Investment Company Fact Book, Fig. 2.5.

links.why: Concentrated passive flows move whole indices, feeding back into prices.
links.stat: Directional; flow-driven. Fed staff research documents “index-inclusion effects”: assets added to an index see valuation, volatility, and comovement effects as passive/ETF flows track it. Source: Fed staff research, FEDS 2018-060 “The Shift from Active to Passive Investing” (Section 2.4, Table 4).

links.why: Energy company earnings and stocks move with the oil price.
links.stat: Energy equities strongly correlated with WTI. Source: S&P DJI, EIA. Fitted over 198 usable daily changes in the train split: slope=+0.002217, |t|=8.1.

links.why: Energy is an S&P sector, so its swings show up in the index during oil shocks.
links.stat: ~3% index weight as of mid-2026 (down from ~4% in the 2022 to 2023 window following the Russia/Ukraine oil-price shock), larger earnings swing. Source: S&P DJI, FactSet. Tested over 199 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=1.4 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: Higher mortgage rates cut household affordability and housing wealth.
links.stat: Mortgage debt is the largest household liability. Source: NY Fed.

links.why: Looser credit conditions expand consumer borrowing capacity and spending.
links.stat: Consumer credit tracks financial conditions. Source: Fed G.19.

links.why: Consumption is ~two-thirds of GDP, so household demand supports corporate earnings and equities.
links.stat: PCE ~68% of GDP. Source: BEA.

links.why: Every dollar that moves into a money market fund is a dollar of deposit funding a bank no longer has. This is deposit flight, and it is what actually killed SVB.
links.stat: US banks lost roughly $875B to $960B of deposits across 2022–23 as cash chased MMF yields (FDIC reports $874.1B to June 2023; Fed H.8 shows $960B, Apr 2022 to Apr 2023). Source: FDIC Quarterly Banking Profile, Federal Reserve H.8.

links.why: Repo is how dealers finance their inventory. If repo funding dries up or haircuts rise, dealers cannot hold bonds, and market liquidity evaporates.
links.stat: Structural. Dealers fund the bulk of their Treasury inventory in repo. Source: NY Fed primary dealer statistics, OFR.

links.why: Stress widens repo spreads and raises haircuts, so the same collateral finances less. Funding tightens exactly when it is needed most.
links.stat: Sign is well established; magnitude is unquantified here. Tested over 197 usable daily changes in the train split: the fitted sign disagrees with the sign shown, but only at |t|=0.3 - too weak to act on (logged as a conflict).

links.why: Banks hold agency MBS as high-quality liquid assets. When those marks fall, so does the bank’s capacity to absorb a run.
links.stat: MBS were a large share of the securities portfolios that generated the 2022–23 unrealised losses. Source: FDIC.

links.why: The Fed bought agency MBS outright in QE and is now letting them run off, which removes the single largest price-insensitive buyer.
links.stat: Fed MBS holdings peaked near $2.7T. Source: Federal Reserve H.4.1.

links.why: Fannie and Freddie have been in federal conservatorship since 2008, with Treasury committed to keeping their net worth positive. Agency MBS trade as near-government paper because of that promise, not because the GSEs are strong.
links.stat: Senior Preferred Stock Purchase Agreements, in force since September 2008. Source: FHFA, US Treasury.

links.why: Banks fund deposit insurance themselves through assessments. When banks fail, the insurance fund pays out and is depleted, and the surviving banks are billed to refill it.
links.stat: The 2023 failures cost the Deposit Insurance Fund $16.7B (finalized at $16.3B) and triggered a special assessment on large banks, per FDIC’s own count; the $20B figure sometimes cited traces to a June 2024 CBO report, not FDIC. Source: FDIC.
